character_and_relationship_context: Aminata Diallo lives in a rented room on the outskirts of Bamako, with no running water. She is the youngest person and only woman on a construction crew, where her master mason, Sékou, calls her 'la petite comptable' and checks her arithmetic as a sign of quiet trust. She double-checks load-bearing estimates, a habit born from watching her mother lose a market stall to a miscalculated loan. Aminata's mother died when she was twelve, and her father later sold his tools to pay for a funeral and never held a trowel again. She secretly saves for an accounting course and hides an emergency fund under a floorboard. She also plans to bring her younger sister to live with her, but does not speak of it. She has a tendency to skip the tea stop on Fridays, having done so at least four times this month, and she always walks to work despite having bus fare, leaving the ticket unused. She has never taken the bus home on a Friday, preferring to save the ticket for a weekday when she is more tired. The tea vendor is a familiar face she passes each Friday, but they exchange only nods. Her younger sister depends on monthly remittances sent through a money transfer service.
objective_situation: It is Friday evening, and Aminata is walking home from the construction site. The air is cooling, and the street is filling with people. She passes the tea vendor near the corner, where the smell of ginger and mint drifts toward her. In her pocket she has the exact coins for a small cup of tea, which she rarely allows herself. In her other pocket, she has the bus ticket she saved by walking to work that morning. The bus would get her home before dark, leaving her more time to study. She stops for a moment, looking at the vendor, then at the empty street stretching home.
state_and_available_memories: Her shoulders ache from carrying cement bags, and her feet are blistered from the long day. She is thirsty but not desperately so, and the smell of tea is enticing. She is aware that darkness will fall in about forty minutes, and the walk home takes thirty. The scent of ginger and mint pulls her back to a memory of her mother brewing tea on a Friday evening after a long week at the market. The bus ticket in her pocket reminds her of the morning she chose to walk instead of using it, saving it for exactly this moment. She also remembers the time she bought a small cup of tea and then had to borrow from her emergency fund when a bus fare increased unexpectedly. She recalls the year her mother walked two hours each way to save transport money, only to lose the stall anyway.
name: Aminata Diallo
